note: Maintainer-written statements of source facts, with locators to the original arXiv v1 HTML. These are fixed inputs, not the original prose. Locators are provenance references only; the original document is not provided as a task asset.

facts.statement: FTCT models knowledge as a directed graph G=(V,E). The vertices V are a subset of the alphabet V_all := {A,B,...,Z,a,b,...,z}. Each vertex v has a value q(v) from a set VALS(v) ⊂ Z. Each edge e=(v1,v2) carries an operation op(e) with q(v2) = op(e) ∘ q(v1), and op(e) is only an addition or a subtraction (such as +a or −b). The chains are T(G) := {[v1,...,vn] | n ∈ N, (vi,vi+1) ∈ E}. The depth N of G is the length of the longest chain in T(G).

Training data (D_train) leaves out the longest chains. It uses child chains of length M < N from T(G) instead, merged in order with M' noise vertices drawn from V_all − V. Child-chain values follow the edge operations: the first is drawn uniformly from VALS(u1), then q_{i_h} = op((u_{h−1},u_h)) ∘ q_{i_{h−1}} for h = 2..M. Noise vertices get random values. A training sequence is seq := [v1,q1,...,vm,qm] with m = M+M'. Testing data (D_test) uses the longest chains (length N) from T(G), with no noise: seq := [v1,q1,...,vN,qN]. The authors state that models trained on D_train have not seen the complete test chains, either as reasoning paths or as few-shot examples.
locators: Appendix B, A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1 and equation A2.Ex1

facts.statement: A few-shot document joins k sequences that share the same vertex order, separated by newline tokens: doc^k := [seq^(1), \n, ..., \n, seq^(k)], with seq^(i) := [v1, q1^(i), ..., vL, qL^(i)]. L is m or N (training or testing sequences), and k runs from 0 to K. The input is inp^k := doc^k + [v1, q1^(k+1)] and the label is lab^k := [v2, q2^(k+1), ..., vL, qL^(k+1)]. The model generates lab^k autoregressively; k = 0 means there are no preceding examples. A downstream step turns sequences into natural-language-like sentences, adding punctuation and context tokens and stating the reasoning goal first (e.g. 'H=?: ... A=110, ... B=111, ...'). These processed versions are written inp~^k and lab~^k. A decoding function dec(lab~) := lab = [v2,q2,...,vN,qN] recovers the vertex-value information.
locators: Section 3.2 Step 2, S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1 with equations S3.Ex1 and S3.Ex2

facts.statement: The testing criteria are the compositional-reasoning metrics of Section 4.1, evaluated on (inp~^k, lab~^k) from D_test. (a) Whole chain accuracy: dec(model(inp~^k)) contains all elements of dec(lab~^k) in a correct order. (b) Testing vertices accuracy: the model correctly outputs all vertices in dec(lab~^k). (c) Testing values accuracy: the model outputs the correct values of intermediate vertices when given correct preceding reasoning paths from D_test. For example, prompted with '... A=100, ... B=', the output counts as accurate if and only if the next token is '101' (for the paper's Figure 1 structure).
locators: Section 4.1 list items S4.I1.ix1.p1, S4.I2.ix1.p1, S4.I2.ix2.p1

facts.statement: The training (in-distribution) criteria are introduced in Section 4.3. (a) Validation loss: tracks the validation loss during training. (b) Training vertices accuracy: how well the model imitates the vertex order from few-shot examples sampled from D_train. (c) Training values accuracy: whether the model outputs correct values of child-chain vertices, given preceding reasoning paths sampled from D_train.
locators: Section 4.3 list items S4.I3.ix1.p1, S4.I3.ix2.p1, S4.I3.ix3.p1

facts.statement: The training objective is L_train := −E_{lab~,inp~ ∼ D_train} Σ_{k=0}^{K−1} Σ_{t=1}^{d^k−1} log P_model(lab~^k_{t+1} | inp~^k + lab~^k_{1:t}), where d^k is the length of lab~^k. The empirical version averages over B sampled items (−(1/B) Σ_{b=1}^{B} ...). The source does not explicitly tie the Table 1 'validation loss' to this formula on held-out data.
locators: Appendix A.1, A1.SS1.p1 and equation group A1.Ex1

facts.statement: Section 4.3 / Table 1 compares models trained on FTCT with causal structure depth N = 5. The body text says 'a child chain length of 3'; the caption says 'child chain length upper bound M=3'. The models are GPT-2-like Transformers (TF) with different numbers of layers and heads (3L3H, 2L2H, 2L1H, 1L2H, 1L1H) and MLPs of different depths (4L, 2L). The 'Training' columns are in-distribution criteria (validation loss, training vertices acc, training values acc). The 'Testing' columns are compositional-reasoning criteria (testing vertices acc, testing values acc, whole chain acc). The table shows only the performance of models prompted by CoT with the optimal shots number. The 'Params' column gives parameter counts.

Transformer implementation: GPT-2 architecture as implemented by Hugging Face, with 720-dimensional embeddings and a 2048-token context window. Token indices follow the GPT2Tokenizer mapping for encoding and decoding. The optimizer is AdamW with learning rate 5e-5. Appendix G.1 does not give training steps, batch size or seeds.

MLP implementation: sliding windows cap the input length. The authors motivate this by stating that a 1-shot CoT prompt suffices for optimal model performance and that long inputs can hurt training efficiency and accuracy. Window sizes of 150, 200 and 300 tokens were tried and the best-performing size was kept; the source does not say which size each MLP row used. The input concatenates one-hot encodings of the tokens, 503 dimensions per token, so about 1e5 dimensions at window size 300. The hidden size is 1000, the number of layers varies, and the output has 50257 dimensions (the GPT2Tokenizer vocabulary), with near-zero weights on unused tokens. The optimizer is AdamW with learning rate 5e-5.

Table 1 values as printed. Columns: Params | Train valid loss | Train vertices acc | Train values acc | Test vertices acc | Test values acc | Test whole acc. TF 3L3H: 54M | 1.446 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.996 | 1.000 | 0.996. TF 2L2H: 48M | 1.433 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000. TF 2L1H: 48M | 1.436 | 0.870 | 1.000 | 0.768 | 1.000 | 0.766. TF 1L2H: 42M | 1.559 | 0.138 | 0.994 | 0.776 | 1.000 | 0.776. TF 1L1H: 42M | 1.624 | 0.025 | 0.974 | 0.026 | 1.000 | 0.022. MLP 4L: 145M | 3.464 | 0.063 | 0.104 | 0.484 | 0.290 | 0.002. MLP 2L: 143M | 2.147 | 0.065 | 0.146 | 0.850 | 0.346 | 0.022. The machine-readable copy with per-cell locators is ftct_table1_values.csv plus ftct_table1_manifest.json.

Shot-count context (not a statement about Table 1). The source does not state which shot count was used for any Table 1 row, nor how it was selected. Related evidence: Section 4.1 / Figure 2 reports k-shot CoT results (k = 0..4) for 3-layer 3-head Transformers trained on several settings (N = 5, 10, 15; M = 2, 3, 4, 6), which include the same nominal N = 5, M = 3, 3L3H configuration; the source does not say whether that is the same trained model as the Table 1 3L3H row. There, whole chain accuracy is low with zero-shot prompts, rises with more shots, and gains plateau or decline after one shot. In Appendix K the authors state that testing performance peaks at 1-shot and diminishes thereafter, explaining it by extra CoT examples increasing the train/test dissimilarity; in Appendix G.2 they state that a 1-shot CoT prompt suffices for optimal model performance. None of these statements identifies the Table 1 shot count, so it must not be asserted.

Table 1 aggregation is unstated. The table and its caption give no number of runs, seeds, causal-structure resamples, standard deviations or evaluation sample sizes. By contrast, Appendix H.1 says the Figure 3 curves average 5 changed causal structures and report standard deviations. That protocol is not stated for Table 1 and must not be assumed for it.

Optimal-shot condition with unstated details. Table 1 shows each model only at 'the optimal shots number', but the source states neither the shot count used for any row nor the selection rule: not the candidate k range for Table 1, not whether one shot count was chosen per model or per metric column, and not which data or metric decided the optimum. The reported values are therefore post-selection (best-case) summaries. Writers must not assert a specific Table 1 shot count (e.g. 'Table 1 uses 1-shot prompts').

Several details of the validation loss are unstated: the data it is computed on, its normalization (the stated objective sums over shots and label tokens rather than averaging per token), the log base, and the training step at which it was recorded. The loss values therefore cannot be converted to per-token perplexity, and loss is on a different scale from the accuracies. There is also a minor notational inconsistency in Appendix A.1: the sampled set is indexed k = 1..K, while the sum runs over k = 0..K−1.

The meaning of M = 3 is ambiguous. The Table 1 caption says 'child chain length upper bound M=3', and Appendix H.1 says 'maximum child chain lengths (M)'. Section 4.3 says 'a child chain length of 3', and Appendix B defines child chains as having length M. It is unclear whether training child chains all have length 3 or at most 3.

Whole chain accuracy is defined in two ways. Section 4.1 and Appendix H.1 use containment: the generation contains all label elements in a correct order. The testing loss in Eq. (3.1) and Appendix A.2 uses exact equality: 1{dec(model(inp~^k)) = dec(lab~^k)}. The source does not say which one produced the Table 1 'Whole acc' column, beyond the caption's reference to the Section 4.1 criteria.

Scope: the seven model rows of the Table 1 architecture comparison (N = 5, M = 3) and their definitions. There is no new training, inference or replication. Out of scope: other figures and tables, the GPT-2-small/large experiments (Appendix J), and mechanism experiments. These may be named only as the authors' context, as allowed by the fact sheets.

Comparability caveat (maintainer audit of source facts). The rows are not matched on parameter count or input representation. The reported sizes are TF 42M to 54M and MLP 143M to 145M, all rounded to millions. 2L2H and 2L1H are both printed as 48M, and 1L2H and 1L1H both as 42M. The MLPs see a sliding window of one-hot tokens (window chosen from {150, 200, 300} by best performance). The Transformers use a 2048-token context. Table 1 alone therefore cannot attribute differences to attention, depth or head count only.

Reporting rule: each Table 1 cell is one printed point value (3 decimals) of unstated aggregation. Do not add or imply error bars, confidence intervals, repeated-run spreads, hypothesis tests or statistical significance. Do not describe aggregated values as independent runs. Differences in the third decimal (e.g. 1.433 vs 1.436 vs 1.446) should not be read as meaningful rankings.
